Of course, the military commander can warn the military police unit to carry out its tasks according to law and submit to the military prosecution that it pursue further the case on the basis of law. And that is something the commander can do if he observes a certain level of -- that the military police is passive in its activity; namely, he can warn them that they should be more active in their area of activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of difficulties, objective circumstances and difficulties during cross-examination which made command and control more difficult under the circumstances that may have dominated in the Dubrovnik operation. Now, do these difficulties in any way diminish command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that to the regret of military commanders, all the objective difficulties which prevent them from being successful in their command do not prevent them from being fully responsible for the actions of their subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the issue of resubordination which you discussed in cross-examination, making command and control more difficult, were decisions within the 2nd Operational Group concerning resubordination, did those decisions lie with the commander of the operational group, General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If any resubordination of subordinate units of the 2nd Operational Group are in question, then this was in the exclusive responsibility of the commander of the 2nd Operational Group. If, however, the question concerns a resubordination among the units of the 9th VPS, then that would be under the authority of the commander of the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That concludes my redirect. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, I'm very pleased to be able to say that your evidence has come to an end. You are free to leave the Tribunal and return to Slovenia, if that is your wish. May we thank you for your assistance and your patience over these many days. Thank you. If you could leave now with the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I very much thank the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, that is the -- we propose that that is the last witness to be called by the Prosecution, General Zorc. There are other matters which I believe need to be raised concerning, perhaps, last-minute submissions and some outstanding issues. I was informed that this would be the time that we would have an opportunity to raise such issues and if perhaps there were other issues about -- perhaps I misunderstood -- but scheduling matters, that it would also be raised during the remainder of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the issue -- on other issues -- sorry, on issues concerning matters that the Prosecution would seek to have tendered or documents seek to have tendered at this stage, I have asked my colleagues who have been able to work with it while I was in court to present the submissions, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'd like to clear up a few matters which are here for identification at this time. There are four exhibits, P5, 6, 7, 8 for identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, say again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They should be MFI 5678 or P5, 6, 7, 8 for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Those exhibits were introduced into evidence through Mr. Hvalkof on page 2125. Actually on pages 2124 and 2125, there was some discussion that those -- I think Defence counsel first thought those were exhibits, but it was stated that those were documents for identification, and then the Court admitted them. So they are duplicative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So they are exhibits, but separately they have been marked for identification. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. They are now tabs 4, 5, 6, and 7 of P61, which is the Hvalkof binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, are you saying you want them now exhibited twice, or that you no longer --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, no, there's no need to have both. Since they're already in through Mr. Hvalkof, we could just delete those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will remain marked for identification as 5, 6, 7, and 8 and will not be exhibits, then, in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But as part of P61 they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The next is exhibits for identification P84, P86.1, P86.2, and P86.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As a matter of background, P84 was marked for identification. It is a hospital document that was prepared in 2004, in February of 2004. It concerns a witness's 1991 hospital treatment. And if you recall, that's the one that describes a wound in the left leg, even though the witness testified that the wound was in his right leg. P86.1 is a Croatian government disability decision, and within that document it indicates right leg. P86.2 is a Croatian government record. It's a findings and opinion which also indicate right upper leg. P86.3 is a handwritten version of P86.2. It was illegible. Since it was a set, it was left with the other two. During the testimony, the witness Mr. Vlasica testified about being struck with shrapnel in the right upper leg. And he testified about that on pages 3.323 and during cross-examination on 3.432. He even on that page 3.432 offered to show his leg, take his pants down and show his leg and show the injury, which he wasn't taken up on that. During cross-examination, counsel accused the witness of being involved in a forgery, of being involved in perjury, and uttering a forged document. And that's on pages 3.438 to 3.449. It was objected to as having -- and questioned what the basis was. Counsel then offered his basis and views and opinions on why he felt the document was falsified. That's on pages 3.439 and 3.441. The witness then stated that he obtained the hospital records from the hospital, and that the original records are at the hospital if anyone wants them. They're available at the hospital. That's at pages 3.444. To complete this witness, we went past the normal time allotted to our case, we went about 10 or 15 minutes past, and there was not enough time to argue the admissibility of those four documents. It was indicated that the argument would continue the following Wednesday. That was the week where the accused was going to be examined on Monday and Tuesday, and the proceedings would resume on Wednesday. This incident -- testimony occurred on a Friday. We contacted the doctor by telephone to determine the validity of that document that night or a few nights later, and the document read the document to us over the telephone, that he in fact had signed it. Attorney Somers and an investigator then visited the doctor and they saw copies of the original medical reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you giving evidence from the bar table at the moment, Mr. Weiner, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Explanation. I'm going to turn in a document, a statement from a witness as well as medical records, and I'm going to request that they also be admitted. And I've got a basis to -- or I'm going to attempt to provide a basis for admission of those documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, you're out on the edge, as some would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re then visited the doctor with an investigator. And he received a statement from the doctor. The doctor reviewed P84 for identification; said it was, in fact, his signature; said that he did in fact draft the document. He had the medical records there from the hospital. They all reviewed the records, and the records he had previously supplied to the OTP were in fact the records from the hospital. I would like to show you these documents at this time. It is a document from the doctor as well as five medical records from 1991 marked A through E indicating the injury to the witness. And those that discuss exactly the injury all indicate that it's on the right upper leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What basis do you say these can be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, these documents are admissible pursuant to Rule 89(C). Rule 89(C), as the Court knows, says "a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." In Prosecutor versus Galic, the interlocutory appeal on 7 June 2002 at paragraph 31 indicates "a document may be admissible" - and that was a hearsay -- a document following a hearsay exception - "if it was not prepared for the purposes of legal proceedings." And that case was then followed in Prosecutor versus Milosevic, the interlocutory appeal, on 30 September 2003. In paragraphs 11 through 14, the Court followed the Appeals Chamber again followed its previous decision from Galic. As these 1991 medical records were not prepared in anticipation of litigation, they should be admitted, especially as it follows and corroborates the testimony of the witness. The doctor's statement is different. It was drafted in the presence of a Prosecutor and an investigator. It's an explanatory or clarifying document. It's there to show that there was no falsity or forgery involved, that Dr. Segedin did in fact draft and sign the document, which is P84 for ID. That is his own letter. In this case, there was serious allegations made by Defence counsel. Dr. Segedin 's statement clarifies the issue and shows that the allegations were without merit. Dr. Segedin 's statement should be admitted because otherwise, if it isn't, the Chamber is left with a false picture of the circumstances, and a witness is being placed in a false light without any valid basis. Due to the special situation, it is our view that Dr. Segedin 's statement should be admitted; based on Rule 89(C), those five records from 1991, those five medical records should be admitted, and also the four documents which are now P for identification, the one, P84, and the P86.1, .2, and .3 should also be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there have been several inaccurate interpretations by my colleague right now. And there have been several inaccuracies that are unfortunately of a material nature. So I'll start with what was said at the outset. First of all, the Defence objects to the admission of any written statement or any sort of document such as have been distributed to the Trial Chamber a while ago. First of all, it is fundamentally inaccurate and surprising from my learned friend - I'm talking about the Croatian statement and its translation as well as five other documents. It is quite inaccurate that these documents speak about the right leg. If my colleague had had a more careful look, he would have seen easily what the documents say. But I'll come to a little later. I'll start with a statement, Your Honours. There is no legal basis for this statement by witness, Dr. Jaksa Segedin, to be admitted into evidence. The reasons are as follows: The first time the Defence teams saw this statement by witness Jaksa Segedin was yesterday at quarter past 2.00. We only received this document yesterday and not earlier. Secondly, Your Honour, as for the substance of this statement and the attached documents as well as all the documents that my learned colleague refers to, this has a direct bearing to the very substance of the indictment against our client. One of the three allegedly wounded persons is also the person under discussion here, Ivo Vlasica. The position taken on that and the decision taken on that has a most direct bearing on the nature of the indictment against General Strugar. Documents are being tendered into evidence of an unknown nature. These are mere extracts from documents, and nothing is said about the general nature of these documents or who authored them. In addition to that, Your Honours -- these are merely portions of various documents. In addition, and this is very important, in a situation where we are looking at documents and testimonies that have a key significance as to whether Ivo Vlasica had been wounded or not, the Defence is unable to verify in any way whatsoever what we have in front of us now. We have no possibility of cross-examining this witness or ascertaining what these documents are, who they were authored by, and what exactly they describe. Your Honours, the rules as well as the established practice of the International Criminal Tribunal do not allow for this sort of statement to be admitted into evidence, at least not based on the arguments put forward by my learned friend and colleague. To my great satisfaction, he quoted the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Galic case dated the 7th of June 2002 quoting paragraph 31 of that decision. Unfortunately, Your Honours, he failed to read the paragraph to the very end. If he had done that, he probably would have included the following: [In English] [Previous translation continues] "...a written statement given by a prospective witness to an investigator of the OTP under Rule 89(C) in order to avoid stringency of Rule 92 bis." [Interpretation] There is no method, no way of admitting a statement into evidence like this. This is the statement of a witness who has not appeared before the Court, and the statement is given by someone whom we will not have a chance to examine on the substance of his statement. Speaking about the very substance of these documents, Your Honours, there is something that appears to be an extract from a protocol. The document marked as A and the document marked as B is a case history of a disease. Both documents in the legal practice of the former Yugoslavia represent formal documents to prove illness or injury as well as the exact time it occurred. They have a formal value, both these documents, Your Honours, the document marked as A as well as the document marked as B in the attachment. What we can read there, if we look at the English interpretation of the document is "Segedin Jaksa", which is means an explosive wound to the left leg, Your Honours -- the left leg. That being the first document, the protocol marked as A. The second document is a case history of the illness. The first page of the Croatian version also states "sinistri," the Latin for left. This is in handwriting. I believe the English translation reflected this. In the left upper corner of the English translation, "vulnus sclopetarium femoris sinistri," and sin, obviously, is short for left. Further down, Your Honours, on page 2 of the case history -- I've already said was we can read on page 1 -- if we look on page 2, towards the bottom of the page, there is something added in handwriting or rather typewritten, it's a description of an injury stating in B/C/S: "Vlasica," -- based on clinical findings -- "this is a tangential entry-and-exit wound to the side and in the upper third of the left leg." Your Honours, this whole story is about a left leg. Unfortunately, the translation that you were given which refers to that specific page what we find stated there is -- if you look at the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have an official translation. It does not say left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 3 of the English. Case history is page 2. It's B3. It says "Patient History and Findings, Vlasica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the translation that appears, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, had I had an opportunity, I would have completed what I was saying. Unfortunately, a translation that was done for the OTP - for some frivolous reason probably - and we are talking about the difference between the left leg and the right leg. The translation that you have in front of you, indeed, it does not say the left upper leg. But in the original of that translation, and that must be it, it is clearly stated: The left upper leg. So please, if there is any doubt as to what I'm reading from and what I'm showing to the Chamber, perhaps we can give it to the interpreters in this courtroom and have the matter resolved. Therefore, the translation is erroneous. Even in the other document, it says the left upper document. Even in that other document, although my learned friend on page 51, line 1, states all five documents. Only the right leg. Unfortunately, Your Honours, that is not the case. This is entirely erroneous, and if there is even the slightest doubt about my own translation of the case history, can we please enlist the assistance of the interpreters. To our great fortune, there is quite a sufficient number of those in this courtroom. Therefore, Your Honours, further down -- Your Honours, if you can look at the document marked as C, the statement that was given. And according to that statement, this is a statement by a man named Stjepan Bogdanovic, Dr. Stjepan Bogdanovic. If you look at the translation marked as C, in your translation it says signature of a doctor, without specifying which doctor or who. Unfortunately, the stamp on this statement marked as C, the document marked as C, is indeed a stamp that belongs to a man named Stjepan Bogdanovic. However, the signature on this document is one that belongs to a person named Dr. Jurkovic. So it seems that one person stamped the document and a different person signed it. Now, what is actually in that statement, in that document, and what the truth is about the entirety of that document, it is impossible to tell on the basis of this. So it is up to you, Your Honours, to be the judge of that. And then the last document marked as D, Your Honour, there is nothing at all, nothing as to whether it was the right leg or the left leg. Nothing at all. I assume my learned friend and colleague left this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The English translation which is page 3 on D, it says under x-ray report and opinion: "The image of the D/right/thigh does not show any fractures or foreign bodies." So the English translation indicates that it indicates the right--

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm talking about, what I'm talking about is the document marked as E, although my colleague said when I said E, it was said D. I didn't mean D. I meant E; the document marked as E. There is nothing whatsoever about that in the document marked as E. Your Honours, admitting something like this into evidence is in a grave collision with the established practice of the International Criminal Tribunal firstly, and secondly with the established facts. What these documents indicate is unacceptable in every way. Your Honours, may that please be taken into account. Besides, when you make a ruling, I believe it would be interesting or helpful to look at Document D71 which is a verdict of the Dubrovnik municipal courts related to the things that happened on the 6th of December 1991. In that judgement, the same man who was allegedly wounded is referred to as Ivo Vlasica, a child born in 1978. Who is this person? What's at stake here, Your Honours? I believe it is not acceptable to proceed in this way and have any of these admitted into evidence. Thank you very much for your attention, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could I respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there something you wanted in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I may. I would like to read a portion of paragraph 31 of the Galic decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can just leave it to the Chamber to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it's clear that what it says here. Although in this case, in the Galic case, the documents did not satisfy the standard, it does indicate what does, in fact, satisfy 89(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did it deal with the collision between it and 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. And it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it did --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything else in response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That if you look at Dr. Segedin's statement, he indicates the first document is the log, and that the first document is incorrect, which was the A document. But he indicates that the remaining documents do, in fact, indicate that it is the right leg. I also have if the Court wants a statement of the investigator, Raji Murugan who was with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't offer more documents, Mr. Weiner. Now, the translations, are they official translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you have them verified and resubmitted, please. And the Chamber will propose to reserve its decision on these to be given at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll have our case manager resubmit them to CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But that needs to be done promptly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question of the admissibility of not only the documents from the trial that are marked for identification as 84 and 86.1 to 3, as well as the documents now tendered for the first time, will be reserved and will be the subject of decision when the matter can be considered. Now, is there anything further about documents, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Re has some comments on some of the other documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is taking a time which the Chamber did not anticipate. Yes, Mr. Re. You'll need to be prompt.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. We did discuss this with the legal officer that we wish to tender the outstanding documents, and we asked for a suitable time and we were told it was at the conclusion of Mr. Zorc's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, the Chamber did not anticipate the time that is being taken on these matters or the range of documents. But carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next one should be very, very quick and simple. Those are the colour photographs attached to Exhibit P63.6 which were referred to in Dr. Kaiser's evidence. He promised to produce better-quality colour photographs of the photographs attached to his report. We have produced -- or he has produced 31, I think, of the 74-odd photographs in colour. And I've prepared an index for the Trial Chamber's convenience. And I submit those now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not in principle. In principle, we do not have an objection. However, we have not been given an opportunity to have a look at what is being tendered. If that is the same thing as the photographs that have been admitted into evidence, the black and white photographs, of course we have no objection to that. But as I said, we have not had an opportunity to look at these. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The originals were annexed to Exhibit 63. Mr. Re, you're proposing that they should be part of that annexure or a separate exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If Your Honour looks at the index, it may guide Your Honour in how to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think a separate exhibit is going to be more practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received. I would indicate that should it be the case that the Defence finds that any of these photographs are not what they purport to be, that can be the subject of a specific application. If could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Exhibit Number is P210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next category of documents relates to the Croatian Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments and the outstanding report, P51 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the two earlier reports upon which my learned colleague Mr. Petrovic extensively cross-examined Mr. Vukovic in evidence. That was the October report and the October and November report. The argument concerning the admission into evidence of P51 ID certainly has been delayed for some considerable time, at least since Dr. Kaiser gave his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We were going to hear further from Dr. Kaiser. That is not to happen, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. The situation was Dr. Kaiser was -- there was a discussion as to whether he would prepare an additional report in which he would distinguish the damage in his document from the damage in the larger document, P51 ID. Dr. Kaiser has provided the Prosecution with a document which is not really in an admissible sort of form, but would certainly form the basis of a submission or a table which we will produce basically in our 98 bis response to the -- what we anticipate will be the Defence's 98 bis response. In our submission, that particular document that Dr. Kaiser produces wouldn't -- shouldn't affect the issue of the admissibility of P51 ID because it is merely a filtering exercise and there has been a great deal of cross-examination in relation to those two particular areas of damage. And at the end of the day, the Prosecution submits it's really a matter of submission by comparing the two. And of course, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What are you now proposing, that you tender MFI 51 as an exhibit? Is that what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, in addition, the two earlier reports which preceded it, the front covers of which my learned friend Mr. Petkovic tendered into evidence during cross-examination of Mr. Vukovic I think two weeks ago; D57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you remind me why only the front covers were tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, Mr. Petrovic at the time told the Trial Chamber or seemed to intimate that it was the first time he had seen these documents, and then cross-examined Mr. Vukovic for about 20 minutes or so on the table inside those documents, the 45 buildings referred to. However, both these documents are on the Prosecution exhibit list. The October report was 56 on the 65 ter and the October/November report was number 350 on the list. And they are both disclosed to the Defence on the 27th of August last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis do you say the fact that they were the subject of cross-examination makes them admissible? Or is there some other basis upon which you seek to tender them?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The basis is that the basis of the admissibility of the whole of P51/ID which is the relevant probative and which I can certainly address on -- We say the three of them, because of the nature and the extent of cross-examination of the three people who gave evidence about P51/ID - that's Mr. Vukovic, Dr. Kaiser, and Mrs. Peko - has put into issue when the damage occurred in a way that wasn't anticipated at the beginning of the trial. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How can you say that? There was shelling over three months. You've got a report which is dealing with the effects of that shelling. And you seem surprised there should be dispute as to the contents of the report as relevant to what occurred on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My understanding of -- the reason why the Prosecution took the approach was because the Defence counsel had informed Mr. Kaufman they were not opposing the admission into evidence of the Institute's report. And we've took that approach. There was no agreement as to damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was objection to the 51 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was afterwards. We at the time considered there was not going to be an objection, which is why we didn't push the earlier two reports because the third one, P51/ID, was the wrap-up report of all three. The objection in the cross-examination in relation to P51/ID, in our submission, makes the earlier two relevant for the filtering process. Because the October one lists I think 17 or 10 specific buildings - that was the one that the front cover was put into evidence; the next one lists the 45 buildings upon which Mr. Petrovic cross-examined Mr. Vukovic as to they were damaged in October or November or December. And if you look at the two together, you can see the damage in October as listed in the report which was published at the end of October, the damage which was recorded as having occurred in October-November as published in the second report which was prepared in the last week of November. Then you've got the third report from the beginning of January which is all three. And by comparing the three, you can quite easily, the Prosecution can quite easily submit -- if you look at the November report, you can see this damage is recorded. If you look at the December report, you can see there is further damage recorded on all of the 45 buildings which are the subject of the October-November report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there evidence that there was a complete examination of all damage at about the end of November, and all of that is included in the report which is the second of those that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. But the evidence in that report would be of examining 45 buildings which have been -- of which -- evidence has been basically given of almost every one of those buildings. Those were, for example, the buildings in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That deals with 45 buildings. And the one in October deals with how many buildings?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It deals with seven specific buildings, the Rupa museum, the synagogue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Seven, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Franciscan monastery bell tower --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. The point I'm making is there's an enormous gap between that and the number of buildings that are in the MFI 51 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. Well of course, because the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But the problem is that you haven't yet - speaking for myself only - been able to demonstrate that the buildings, other than those for a moment that are in these two further reports you refer to, that the buildings the subject of the MFI51 were not damaged before 6 December 1991. That's your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only way we could do that, some 12 and a half years later would be to call each and every building owner to say whether or not his or her building was damaged on that day or before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have to say I understood during his evidence that Dr. Kaiser said he had done it, and he would come and inform the Chamber about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think it was Dr. Kaiser who said that. I think the representation may have been from someone else. The expectation was that Dr. Kaiser would so to speak authenticate the report, based upon the way we thought the case was going with agreements with the Defence. Had we known otherwise, we would have started calling other authors. As it was, we had a representative sample: Mr. Vukovic, one of the authors; the collaborating member, Mrs. Peko; and a consultant, Dr. Kaiser. So we got three out of the people who actually worked on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As a quick indication of my personal thinking, all three of those witnesses say "we looked in December." They did not look in November or October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, that's quite correct. But you have reports done by the institute of the damage that occurred earlier. And if you look at the reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You made a statement there that doesn't seem to have any foundation in the evidence. Where is there evidence that either or both of those reports were exhaustive of damage at the time they were made?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There isn't that, but there is evidence the fact that reports were made of damage to buildings in October and November. Of course, it's not exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it's not exhaustive, how does it help anybody reach a conclusion about what occurred on the 6th of December except, perhaps, in respect of those particular buildings that are the subject of those two reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's as far as we can put it. We can't put it any higher than there were 45 buildings in the October-November report, and seven buildings in the earlier report, subtract the damage listed in those two, and you can see it's cumulative in the third report which lists far more extensive damage, for example on the Franciscan monastery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're limiting your case to those buildings, your position might change dramatically. But you're not, as I understand it. I haven't heard a hint of it, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, because the schedule to the indictment is based upon the institute report. That was a prosecutorial decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What has been crystal clear in the evidence is the Institute report is not a report of damage which occurred on the 6th of December, it is a report of damage in the months of October, November, and December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you go to -- Mr. Vukovic, for example, he gave evidence of the methodology and how he was able to say that the damage occurred on the 6th of December in the buildings in which he examined. In every case - Dubrovnik is a small place - he said there was someone there or someone next door who would point out the damage which occurred on that day and was able to distinguish it from damage which occurred earlier. Now, in a place which has been subject to several specific bombardments, there is really, in my submission, the indicia of reliability is someone is saying This was damaged on the 6th, and this particular thing was damaged on a different occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's one level --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Re please kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the subject of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic's?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any of that evidence. But it is at a different and significantly less level conviction, in respect of the buildings which are the subject of no direct evidence whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution says that the institute report is corroborative of the entirety of the Prosecution evidence from a number of witnesses as to the extensiveness of damage to the Old Town on the 6th of December and indicates if you look through the report damage that clearly was not there before. The videos - that's the P145, P66 and P78 - clearly show contemporaneous damage. It's a smouldering town. It's consistent broadly with what is in the institute report, the December report. You've had specific evidence from a number of witnesses who were there, including, of course, Dr. Kaiser, Mr. Vukovic, Mrs. Peko, Mr. Jusic, Mr. Gobisic, Witness A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, no need to go on. We appreciate all of that. And I have tried succinctly to put to you at least my fundamental reservation about your position. While the Prosecution maintains its allegations in respect of all the buildings listed in the report that is marked for identification as 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just excuse me for one moment while I consult with Ms. Somers on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution -- while the schedule is, of course, the foundation for our case on property damage, the Prosecution of course acknowledges that the end of the case, which is basically today, we're not in a position to say that each and every one of those 450 buildings listed in the report and the schedule we can prove beyond a reasonable doubt were damaged on the 6th as opposed to an earlier day. What we can say if you look at the report it is corroborative of the general thrust of evidence of extensive damage to the Old Town on that particular day. We will certainly be submitting in the chart which we've given a copy to my learned friend, anticipated chart of the evidence of all the buildings of which we have direct damage. I haven't totalled it up since Mr. Vukovic gave his evidence, but the anticipation before was about 140 to 150 buildings. We have to go back for our submissions to carefully itemise each one of them and plot it on the computer-generated chart. What we wish to do is to go through each of the buildings which we say we have proved through direct testimony of all the witnesses I have listed before; through looking at the videos; through all the evidence and say look at the institute report. That points to this building, this building, this building, and this building, thus corroborating the nature, the type of damage, the holes in the roof being consistent with shelling, the cracks in the walls, the missiles or whatever, to say the report is corroborative and consistent with the buildings we can prove. We don't say we can prove 450. We say we can prove -- I can't give you a figure, but it's over a hundred. And we want to use the institute report to corroborate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the Prosecution's position, why is it not amending the indictment to limit its case, instead of leaving all these other buildings in issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What we -- we can certainly at the moment stipulate or enter into talks for stipulation following the close of the Prosecution's case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have had talks on damage since before this trial commenced, but certainly during it, some involving the Chamber; and they have been fruitless because the Prosecution has persisted at one end at the total number of buildings in the indictment, and the Defence has persisted in a quite distinct position at the other end of the spectrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We certainly hear what Your Honours are saying. We will give very due consideration -- very prompt consideration to what Your Honour is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm conscious of the time. The tapes are about to run out. We must adjourn now for the minimum time to enable the tapes to be changed, and then continue. We must work speedily. I've heard your submissions in respect of these documents. Perhaps Mr. Petrovic might give consideration to those submissions over the break. And we will then hear him. But I would encourage him to have regard to what I have been putting to Mr. Re. And he has no need to go over territory that I've already covered. Some might think I was on your side of the bar table on a couple of occasions there. It was merely to test the propositions that were being put. But at least you can see from that that the Chamber is aware of some of the issues you might be advancing, and there's no need for you to go through all of those again as though we were not aware of them. We will adjourn now and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in line with your instructions, I will try to address you very briefly. The Defence is opposed to having any of these three documents that are being discussed admitted into evidence. In view of your instructions, I shall just outline what I wished to say otherwise, in order to try to finish today. If the grounds for admission is Rule 89(C), I'm talking about three conditions: Relevance; probative value, that is, what is contained in Rule 89(C); and there is a third condition and that is part of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and that is reliability. We can see that in the Tadic decision, the 5th of August 1996, paragraph 7 and 8; the decision from the Delalic case [In English] "Motion of the Prosecution for the Admissibility of Evidence" [Interpretation] dated the 19th of January 1998; also, we can see this in the same decision from the Tadic case. The essence of what is said there is that reliability is an inherent component of the admissibility of evidence. If a document is unreliable, it can neither be relevant nor can it have probative value. In addition to that, Tadic, the 5th of August 1996, in order to assess reliability, the Trial Chamber has to look into the circumstances under which the evidence appeared and then to decide on the matter. I would like to recall the high standards of common-law systems and also I would like to say that in civil-law systems, the standards are not that high, but there are two requirements. One is that the evidence is lawfully obtained, and the second is that the accused is in a position to question it and oppose it. That is Criminal procedure in the European Community, paragraph 4.3.1, page 20. Your Honour, in relation to what is being sought here, we wish to point out that first and foremost, we do not have the ability to actively bring into question any of what is being sought here today. P51 is a compilation of individual notes, 450 of them. This was prepared by certain individuals who did not appear before this Court. They said nothing about the content of these documents, and the Defence simply was not in a position to question in any way what is contained in these documents. More than 80 per cent of it was not something that could be checked before this Court. All of the people who came here barely knew how to react to things that they had participated in themselves, let alone 450 other entries in that document. I'll try to be as brief as possible. First and foremost, there are no legal grounds for admitting into evidence all of this. As for the October and November reports, we do not know who wrote them, how this person wrote them, for what purpose; nothing is known about the photographs, maps, the graphs. Quite simply, as regards everything that is contained in these documents in P51 and then the 80 per cent of the transcripts that were compiled by other persons, we did not have any way of putting questions as to what was contained there. We had no way of challenging it in any way. Quite simply, people who came here would first say that they knew perhaps something about the place where they were, but they didn't know anything else about this. So we simply had no one to put these questions to you; not to mention the other requirements, probative value and reliability that I already referred to. For about 20 days, according to my mathematics, we listened to this courtroom. And it is the position of the Defence that neither one of these two requirements has been met. Your Honour, I can go on at length about this. I have a multitude of arguments in this respect. However, if this is not sufficient for your ultimate decision, we are prepared to make further submissions in writing, if my present submissions are not sufficient to convince you of the fact that what the Prosecution is seeking is wrong from the point of view of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, and also the practice of relevant national jurisdictions. I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. Anything in response Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. If I wasn't clear in my submissions before, the Prosecution was not intending to proffer P51 as primary evidence of proof of damage to each of those buildings which are listed in the schedule. At this stage of the case, the basis for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm glad you added those words. Because until this stage of the case, that's exactly what they have been offered for or what it has been offered for.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise, the way I prepared my submissions, I was slightly taken by surprise. That is the basis on which we offer it into evidence at the moment. It's corroboration of evidence we say which independently proves the property damage through Mr. Jusic or Mr. Grubisic or Mr. Vukovic or whoever. We say if you take the two together, it provides evidence of the extensive nature of damage and take that into account of considering the overall damage and the specific buildings -- which we will, of course, list in the 98 bis response we do. We will list the buildings we say we can prove. And we will then refer them, if the documents goes into 51/ID, as corroboration of the damage which can be independently proved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic did some sums to give a total. But the time that has been spent in the course of this trial over this property issue is a matter of no satisfaction, to put it very mildly, to the Chamber. And it is a great pity that some of these matters were faced more realistically at an earlier stage. But not to be spending all this time on this issue right now, among other things. Is that what you had in mind putting?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. And in relation to Your Honour's other point about -- we will look at amendment. But our primary purpose at the moment during this submission is to submit those which we can prove and those which we will no longer say -- we will no longer rely upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you at least come to that point, it would be of material assistance to everybody, especially the Defence and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was the purpose of preparing the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can see movement out of my right eye. So I better see what Mr. Petrovic has in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, although I wanted to save everybody's time here, obviously I cannot do it. What my learned friend said is absolutely unacceptable. The indictment against our client contains all 450 buildings. How can he say that this was only given by way of illustration or to support other evidence, if this is contained in the indictment, and if the indictment was written on the basis of this document? Thank you. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will reserve its decision in respect of the admissibility of the document marked for identification as P51 and in respect of the motion that the Chamber should receive into evidence Rule 65 ter Document Number 350 and Rule 65 ter Document Number 56. Is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise, it's actually 55, not 56. I have been just been corrected by my case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is there any other matter which the Prosecution would seek to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was one document which we had intended to tender through Mr. Janikot who we didn't call in the end. It was referred to in the evidence of Dr. Kaiser who was cross-examined at page 2468 to 2472. These are the minutes of meetings between UNESCO representatives of whom Dr. Kaiser was one, Mr. Karneze, Mr. Janikot, Mr. Vogeric, with the various Yugoslav and Serbian and republican authorities between the 28th of October and the 2nd of November 1991; Document 03449330 to 9339 in the English translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry to be taking up this much time. What is this all about? You must have seen it yourselves. For some reason Mr. Janikot did not come before this Chamber. What does the Prosecutor want now with Documents 420, 421, and 519? Everything that they wanted to tender through that witness and what pertains to the very essence of what this witness's testimony would be is what they're trying to have admitted into evidence now in this way, which is quite inappropriate, Your Honour. Let us start with Document 421. That is a record of a meeting that was made by someone; we assume that it's Mr. Janikot. And some people took part in this meeting. We don't know anything about this document. Authenticity. Source. Time. Nothing. Your Honours, this is unacceptable. We oppose having any of this admitted into evidence in this way. Had it been necessary, they could have brought in a witness who would have said what this was. This record in its own right does not meet any one of the requirements that I referred to a few minutes ago. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The decision on the admissibility of Documents 65 ter numbers 420, 421, and 519 will be reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just indicate, the original letter we sent to the Defence indicated those three particular ranges. This is actually part of Document 421. It is not actually 420 or 519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I do not understand what you have just said. I understood that you were seeking to tender three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no, only one. I thought I said one document with the ERN ranges of 03449330 to 9339. It's one document which was in within 65 ter exhibit 421, which comprised I think several documents. We are not attempting to tender 420 or 419 as originally indicated to my friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it's pages 03779330 -- sorry, 03449330 to 9339 of the 65 ter Document Number 421. And that decision will be reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask for a clarification now. So the Prosecution does not want 420 and 5-1-9 [as interpreted] to be admitted, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems to be the position, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything else, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not from me. There are some outstanding translations which the case manager has. All from admitted exhibits. Does Your Honour wish me to submit them in Court or through the Registry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Through the Registry, please, yes. Well, then, subject to the issues of the admissibility of those documents and the decisions in respect of them, is that the case for the Prosecution, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may just clarify one point. If in terms of the reduction of the number of structures from the overall 400-something to what the Prosecution submits what in fact has been proven, if it is acceptable for us to handle it within the 98 bis submission with indications of what we will not be proceeded upon, perhaps this would simplify the procedure. And then there would be no need for any further additional submission on that issue other than whatever is argued in 98 bis response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, we can't be in the position of directing you or guiding you what you should do. One course is to amend the indictment. That has procedural implications. Another is to face up to reality if there's a 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And it's just a question of how we handle it, whether we simply indicate in the motion of not proceeding on this or not proceeding on this which I think has been the preferred, or has been a consistent approach we were permitted to use. I think it's a better approach, and I think it would make it easier for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There is nothing further the Prosecution will attempt to put in this case. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the case. Thank you. Now, at this point, clearly there are some outstanding decisions, a number on matters of evidence today and the question of the fitness of the accused to plead which the Chamber has under consideration at the present time. It is convenient at this stage, I think, to try and look at possible stages for the future. This can only be done at this stage on the hypothesis that there should be a finding that the accused is fit for trial. If that isn't the finding of the Chamber, well, then, of course, none of this future contingent planning have any relevance. Should the accused be found fit for trial, it would seem to be a convenient time to quickly look at what might lie ahead. Would the Chamber anticipate a 98 bis submission, Mr. Rodic? The answer, as you've often put to many witnesses, can be yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes or no. One way or the other, Your Honours, the Defence is going to be working on Rule 98 bis and submissions to that effect, if that is the answer you sought. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We somewhat anticipated that might be the case. That being so, we have to look to the time, should the trial continue, when that 98 bis submission would be filed. You would normally have seven days under the Rules. Is there any particular submission about that time? Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't know whether this is the right time, but I would like to take advantage of your question related to 98 bis timing to ask you to make submissions in terms of our further planning for these proceedings, if you believe that this is an opportune moment to deal with such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's what I'm attempting to do at the moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would ask for the following, Your Honours: In view of the fact that the lead Defence counsel in this case will not be in a position to come to Podgorica, or rather his home, by Thursday the 20th of May, what we would kindly ask, Your Honours, is that the Defence be granted time until Monday, the 31st of May for filing its motion in respect of Rule 98 bis. Your Honour, as for the length of our case - and I assume that that is something that you are certainly interested in, providing, of course, that you rule that General Strugar is fit to continue the trial - the Defence wishes to say that the Defence case, as matters stand now, will last up to four weeks including time for cross-examination, to the extent to which and proportionate to what the Trial Chamber allowed the Defence to do during the Prosecution case. So bearing in mind the ratio between the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, that is the time we envisage if we take as a basis the Prosecution case and what was done then. Of course, that would be our upper limit, so to speak. But of course, Your Honour will shorten the time available if you deem it necessary. As for timing, Your Honour, between the present day and the day when the Defence case is supposed to start, we would like to present a few matters that are relevant to your decision. Your Honour, unfortunately Defence teams have far less members and much less resources than our learned friends of the Prosecution do. During these five months or so while we have been here, Your Honour, the Defence worked on investigation, contacts, finding potential witnesses, speaking to them. All of that basically stopped to a significant extent. So what is important for us now, Your Honours, is that between today and the day when the Defence case starts, we have a time period which will make it possible for us to make up for this that was not done due to objective circumstances over these five months, starting from December last year. Your Honour, bearing in mind that our case will go on for up to four weeks, bearing in mind all the constraints that we all have together within the institution of the International Criminal Tribunal, with longer preparations the Defence can shorten its case. But we kindly ask that the minimum time given to the Defence to prepare its case should be six weeks. That would be the bottom line. We really could not prepare our Defence properly in less time than that. Please bear in mind our arguments. Please take them into account, and please meet our request as we've put it forth now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, six weeks from when?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From today, Your Honour. From tomorrow, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought you may have had a future starting date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. McCreath has informed me that the 31st of May is a holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are there any submissions the Prosecution would like to advance? We are looking ahead against the prospect that the accused may not be found fit to plead guilty. In respect of the 98 bis decision, Mr. Petrovic has just put submissions against the contingency that there is found to be a case to answer, and he has looked into the Defence case. On those contingencies, if you can indicate the Prosecution's position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In terms of the time for which their submission is due, if the Chamber is in agreement, the Prosecution does not object. We would ask for ten days in which to file a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the contingent basis on which we've received these submissions, and that is subject to the decision on the question of the fitness to plead and on the 98 bis motion, the Chamber would allow to the Defence until Friday, the 28th of May time to file the 98 bis motion. And then to the Prosecution, until Monday, the 7th of June. I think in each case, that's a day or two short of what was sought, but still a reasonable appreciation of what is involved. And should the eventuality prove to be the case, we would look to commence the Defence case on Monday, the 28th of June, which should accord roughly with what has been sought by way of time. Is that a sufficient indication at the moment for planning purposes? Should, of course, that eventuality occur, there will be need for the Defence to give attention to Rule 65(G) in a fairly tight time span once a decision on Rule 98 bis is delivered. So that needs to be kept in mind. Are there any other outstanding issues?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, sir, not from us. But on that last point that Your Honour just addressed, would there be an indication of how much time between the submission of the 65 ters from the Defence and the commencement of trial? Because that obviously will be the first time the Prosecution has a glimpse at the witness list or anything. I just wondered if you had an idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would hope it may prove possible for information to be shared on an informal basis before there is the formal filing, a course that seems to have been followed by the Prosecution from time to time. And by that means, the prospect of the Prosecution being taken by surprise and, therefore, the presentation of the Defence case interrupted, can be minimised or hopefully avoided all together. And that's why I drew attention to Rule 65(G). And the Chamber would certainly add its anxiety that the time constraints that we will be under, because we are allowing fuller than usual time for preparation of 98 bis by both parties, that they will in turn be responsive to the need to share information about the Defence case, at least informally, at a time which will allow the other side opportunity to be ready to commence and to proceed on Monday, the 28th of June with the hearing of Defence evidence. Could I indicate, because I did not, in response to something put by Mr. Petrovic, that if either side wishes to supplement what has been said in oral submissions about the admissibility of any one of the issues of evidence that were considered today, written submissions will be received from either side on any or all of those matters until Friday of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, on behalf of the Defence, I would like to thank you for your understanding and flexibility in terms of the possible time for preparing our Defence. In addition to that, I must regrettably bring up another subject, and that is Rule 54 bis. Several times we had informal discussions with Ms. Somers asking her to deal with the epilogue of our discussion of 54 bis; that is to say, to give a survey of the documents of the Republic of Croatia provided to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. Regrettably, this has not been done yet, so I just wish to inform you, Your Honours, of the matter, and could we please have some indication of whether this will be done at all; and if so, when. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber are directed the Prosecution to make inquiries. The Prosecution has been make inquiries, but it involved not just this institution but going to the field. And I've indicated to counsel - and it is true, we have been speaking about this - that when I have gotten the feedback, which I think we had a three-week time frame which we are rapidly approaching, any document that approaches or that may, if it appears to even approach, we will certainly be happy to turn over. The question that the Chamber said is if there were an issue about 68 or not, and that really is the thrust of it, that we can come to the Chamber. At this point, I cannot say that there is something that I need to approach the Chamber about. What I will say is I was informed by our head of mission in Zagreb and the Croatian government has informed him that in direct contact with the Defence on this, and my understanding is that there is an arrangement, if I have been given correct information, for the Defence to have produced if they haven't been able to track the documents whatever they have. Again, they have been working directly with the Defence, according to Mr. Mulhajic. We have been working on this. It's a very high priority for the OTP. It involves a lot of searching and record perusals. I want the Chamber to be assured that is certainly and has been underway since the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Clearly, Ms. Somers, it's a matter for concern as the Defence preparation will depend in part on this. So your full attention to the matter would be appreciated by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I just wanted to let the Chamber know also the Defence has been given, apparently, the necessary permission to get from the provider whatever is really being sought. But we will certainly assist in any way that we can do as per the directive of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think I can take the matter further at this point, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just two or three words briefly: We have not yet been in touch with anyone in the Croatian government, not since that day actually because we are here in the courtroom every day, and that's one reason why we couldn't do it. As for information that seems to be in the possession of Ms. Somers, I know nothing about that. I believe that document or the list that was referred to at the time at least should be submitted. If not, we'll ask for whatever they have. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will leave it in the hands of counsel for the moment. That having been said, we will adjourn now for some time.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.46 p.m.
